title: Ideas Needed! Giving your players (and yourself) different experiences each time your game is played.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
Ok, so this is going to be a long post because of the starting ideas listed.
So, the premise of this is that I want to make a game where I don’t know how the game is going to completely unfold, not even as the developer. Since I want to make the type of game that I want to play and I will be spending a significant amount of time testing it, I don’t want to know exactly what is going to happen at every point, where everything is going to be, how to complete every quest, what every NPC is going to say, etc. I want to make my and each player’s experience as potentially different as possible each time the game starts and as it progresses.
For example, I don’t want to start my game and immediately know where my character or party will start, where everything is, where each NPC is, what quests any NPC has, what NPCs will say, where items will be, etc. Obviously, I will still know the bookends of what is possible to exist in the game.
I have quite a few ideas already of how this can be partially achieved. But I would love to hear other suggestions that I can experiment with. Maybe you’ve seen things in games you played. Or maybe you have experimented with some of these things in your own game already. Or maybe you can just brainstorm the “what if” possibilities.
I don’t really want this post to be about debating the merits of these ideas or individual preferences. Although, points about the feasibility of certain ideas would certainly be appropriate along with an estimate of potential level of effort. Especially if it relates to any sort of limitation regarding the game engine itself and not just “that would be a lot of work.”
I already know that some of these ideas would be extremely complicated to implement and bug testing could be challenging.
Also, ideas that require significant departure from the standard RPG Maker default, in-game UI or functionality are welcome and encouraged. Ideas that require custom menus or custom systems like battle, shop processing, etc. should all be on the table.
And ideas don’t have to be limited to the typical RPG Maker “sprite exploring maps” presentation. A game presentation might involve just an overworld map of selectable locations, or simple line paths with locations/destinations, or be mostly text based, or involve button selection options for locations, or other possibilities.
As another caveat, when I use the term “random” that is subject to each person’s interpretation of what is reasonable and appropriate, which will be different from person to person. And there would need to be parameters around how much randomness is incorporated and how random determinations of some things would need to cascade throughout the game.
The more “randomness” you choose to implement, the more careful you would need to be to make sure that there aren’t any contradictions throughout the game, that the player can’t get soft locked at any point, that quests/jobs can be completed, that the game is still balanced, etc.
Please explain your ideas with enough detail that people will get the general idea of what you are suggesting.
Feel free to expand on any of these starter ideas and ask any questions if the idea doesn’t make any sense to you.
So, in no particular order:
Random maps (fixed)
You could make different fixed versions of maps and then randomly select which one the player encounters and that map is then saved in that location
You could do this anytime there is a map transfer event
This could include towns, inns, shops, dungeons, houses, floors, rooms, outdoors, etc.
Dungeon floors could be randomized
Example 1:
Your total game only has 8 Inns, but you make maps for 15 Inns and randomly determine which of those 15 Inns are used for the 8 necessary Inn locations
Example 2:
You have a cemetery location in your game
You make three different versions of the map and then randomly select which one is used for that game when the player gets to that location
Random starting locations
As many as you want to add for increased variety of where the game starts
Players can start in different fixed map locations or specific starting locations might be different based on other random options for that location
Starting location based on character creation
You could change the possible starting location based on certain choices during character creation
Random names for locations
Could have lists of words for possible combination so location names are potentially different from game to game
Random location content generation (for example what town options are present)
Is an Inn present? Where is it?
Are any shops present? What type and where are they?
What NPCs are present and where are they?
What player resources are available outside of shops and where are they?
What other buildings are present and where are they?
What clutter is around the town and where is it?
Could have minimum content parameters as appropriate for the game type to ensure that there are always sufficient resources and options available to the player
Random placement of NPCs (including recruitable NPCs)
Both within a location and across locations
NPCs can be assigned to different locations from game to game
Random determination of what NPCs are encountered (including recruitable NPCs)
Not all available NPCs need to be present in every game
Random determination of NPC details (as applicable)
Name, Portrait, Sprite, Role (General, Recruitable, Merchant, Quest Giver, Lore Provider, Trainer, Quest Related, etc.), Background, Description, Stationary or Mobile, Schedule of when available
Random NPC dialog
Greetings & Farewells, Lore, Hints, General dialog based on NPC details
These are separate from specific dialog needed for things like quests or important information needed to advance the game
Random quests/jobs
Could have a lists of quests/jobs
Not all quests/jobs need to be in each game
Can be optional and repeatable or one time story drive
Quest/Job Givers – who gives what quests/jobs
Details – What to do for what reward?
Random Simple Optional Fetch Example: X: Item, Y: Number, Z: Reward/Pay
You need to bring Y (15) of X (Wood) for Z (5 gold)
Location of items or steps needed to complete quests/jobs could be random
Random placement of items
For Quests
Important game advancing items
Random treasure
In shops and with merchants
So, items that can be found in a town wouldn’t always be exactly the same in the exact same place
Random placement and content of treasure chests or containers
Different locations, types, descriptions, and contents
Random inns
Location, NPCs, Inn Keepers, Layouts
What is bought or sold?
If using traditional RPG Maker maps for Inns, you could have numerous different Inn layout maps created and then select one for that location
Or you could make the shell of an Inn map and then randomly place events for clutter and interactions within the map
Random shops
Location, NPCs, Shop Keeper, Layout
What is bought or sold?
If using traditional RPG Maker maps for Shops, you could have numerous different Shop layout maps created and then select one for that location
Or you could make the shell of a shop map and then randomly place events for clutter and interactions within the map
Random prices
Prices for buying and selling could be within a reasonable range and also affected by different factors like attributes, skills, season, supply and demand, fame or reputation, etc.
Random descriptions of things
Use lists of descriptive words to describe locations, chests, doors, items, NPCs, etc.
Once the descriptions are established they are saved for that thing
Random determination of locks and traps for chests and doors
Locked? Trapped? Both? Mechanical? Magic? Both?
Type? Level? Key?
Random naming of traps
List of possible names (Fire Bomb, Poison Needle, Blinding Powder, Acid Spray, etc.)
Could randomly combine parts of names with lists of agent and mechanism/mode of delivery (ensuring only reasonable combinations)
Could use runes for letters of the alphabet and then randomly assign the runes to each letter at the start of the game. Then the locks/traps names would be presented to the player as a series of runes. But each new game would have the runes assigned to different letters of the alphabet. So, the trap Fire Bomb written in runes would look different each time until you decode it using skills.
Random location of enemies/non-enemy encounters
Types of enemies/non-enemy encounters possible by general location
Random placement in specific locations
List of possible non-enemy encounters that are like skill checks that can be triggered in different locations
So, skill check encounters aren’t always triggered in the same location
Random enemy equipment & treasure
Could have lists of possible treasure associated with each enemy
Based on type, enemies could have random equipment that they use in combat and that is lootable after they are defeated (unless already used in combat)
Random map locations
Placement of entrances to caves, dungeons, ruins, castles, towns, villages, forests, deserts, mountains, lakes, etc.
Random puzzle locations
Puzzles are not always in the same locations
Could have checks in certain places to see if a puzzle is there and then randomly determine what type of puzzle it is
If making a traditional RPG Maker map exploration type of game, you could have these checks trigger a “mini game” on a different map instead of always visually hard mapping the puzzle
You could also make different fixed maps of a location with different puzzles that can be chosen
Random puzzle types and solutions
Puzzles could be for revealing secrets, for removing obstacles, for a secret rewards, for traps, a combination of these, or more
Possible multiple solutions to different puzzles chosen randomly
Design puzzles that can have different solutions randomly determined
Example 1:
Large stone statue standing behind an empty pedestal
Puzzle requires placing a randomly chosen item on the pedestal
Could have lists of item types like weapon, armor, potion, ingredient, magic, etc.
Could have skill check opportunities for the player to get hints about what needs to be placed on the pedestal based on a description of the statue
Skill checks could result in no hints, general hints, or specific hints
But with poor skill check results, even the developer wouldn’t know the exact correct solution without trial and error
Trial and error could have different results depending on the puzzle type
The player could lose access to a secret reward, a trap of some sort could be sprung, a helpful hint message could be triggered, or nothing might happen
Example 2:
Levers or pressure plates need to be pulled or pressed in a certain order
The order could be randomly determined when the puzzle is first accessed and then stays the same for that game so even the developer wouldn’t know the correct order for that puzzle
Incorrect guesses could have random results
Nothing might happen, a trap might be sprung, etc.
Example 3:
There are oddly symmetrical holes in the walls in a room or in different rooms of a dungeon
The holes look like they would be for projectiles but the actual projectile that is required to be placed in the holes is randomly determined when the puzzle is first encountered
Could be arrows, darts, bolts, sling bullets, spikes, etc.
Skill checks could again determine if any hints are available to the player
There is an audible click when the correct projectile is placed in an empty hole
If the player tries the wrong projectile, it won’t fit properly
Once the appropriate projectile has been placed in all the holes the trap is fully set and can be triggered in some way
This could just be a puzzle that is a trap to try to hurt the player or the projectiles could now be imbued with magic as part of the puzzle
If the trap is triggered, the player could be hurt by the magic projectiles, but this is also a reward since the player can now use the magic weapons
Random item names and descriptions
Could have lists of descriptive words to randomly combine for names
Could have lists of random words to generate a description of certain items
Random alchemy
Could have lists of ingredients like plants, gems, etc.
At the beginning of the game, the ingredient names are randomly selected and assigned a purpose that then is applicable throughout the game
So, for each game, the player needs to figure out what ingredient is used for what
So, in one game Willow Flower + Berry Root + Mummy Dust creates a paralyzing agent (potion, powder, etc.) whereas in another game that paralyzing agent might result from Scorpion Venom + Ash Bark
You could also have ingredients that aren’t random and don’t change from game to game
Random names for curses and diseases
Could have lists of possible names or words that can be combined to create names
So, specific curses and diseases could be called different things in different games
Random availability of certain things like certain higher level special items, spells, etc.
It could be possible to play through a game and never find certain things because they just aren’t randomly selected for placement in the game. The King’s Bounty games use this mechanic which includes named items, spells, and even recruitable troops.
Random overarching main quest line
The main quest line could be chosen randomly from a list of possibilities
Even the same main quest could be significantly varied by placement of NPCs and necessary steps to advance and achieve the main quest
Random Guilds
What Guilds are available?
Placement of Guilds?
How to join Guilds?
Quests/Jobs offered by Guilds
Training and equipment offered by Guilds
NPCs located in the Guilds
Random game world dynamics
You could randomly determine the demographics of the game world that then affects how frequently certain types of enemies or NPCs are encountered
What else can you think of?
Thanks in advance for reading this and taking the time to contribute if you have anything to suggest!
Happy game making!

posts.author: ThatIndieSphinx
posts.body:
That is a lot of words and looks like it took a long time to think!
This sort of reminds me of Minecraft world generation, where no two seeds are the same.
I'm not an expert plugins, but I do think it would be awesome if you somehow manage to code a seed input system within the main menu that randomizes the world generation, including maps and structures.
It would definitely require a huge amount of time to script, but would definitely fit what you are looking for.
Add in like a final boss that you have to face off and you would have a terraria/minecraft copy, which would be really amazing.
If the randomized tilesets and generation is too complicated, you could always just create a set of premade maps and randomly fit them together during world creation.
I don't really know how to implement that, it's just me yapping away at my idea, sorry if it doesn't help!

posts.author: Crim_T
posts.body:
Some general thoughts on RPG games and randomness.
In my opinion, one of RPG Makers greatest strength's is how easy it is to have the ability to create a well crafted storyline.  This also goes into one of it's biggest weaknesses, that once you've played through the game once there isn't really much reason to play again.
Have you ever looked at the SAGA line of games?  Specifically Romancing Saga 1, 2 and 3?  They do an excellent job at keeping the plot on track while also randomizing elements.
For example:
Multiple choices for who your main player is.  Each player has their own somewhat unique opening area and plot that eventually leads into the main quest.
Quest lines that are only available for certain HP ranges.  This makes it harder to see all the content in one play through and makes each play through semi-unique.
Skills and leveling are semi randomized.  Being underleveled will actually give you a higher chance to learn new skills.  A great idea for rewarding the player for not grinding.
New Game + content.   The romancing saga 1 remake gives more resources for leveling with each playthrough as well as some quests that are only finishable after multiple games.  Some Rogue-Like games will only unlock the more intersting classes with multiple playthroughs.
If going more in the style of the original Rogue game, it may be interesting to check out the wiki on Visustella's Random Dungeon Maps.  Though I know you also are learning javascript so would be unlikely to go down that route.

posts.author: Piyan Glupak
posts.body:
One of the things that I do for repeat playability is to give the player a choice of party members, choosing from more classes than there are party members. For instance, my current project has 2 compulsory members who are best left in the reserve party, plus 4 from a choice of 14 (male and female actors of 7 classes).
The two compulsory actors are weak, and are used to hang the story on. The thief's presence is necessary for a number of doors. The healer does her work before and after battles.
Magic using classes have the ability to learn
some
of each others spells, but usually do better using their own. It goes without saying that enemies are frequently more vulnerable to some elements than others.
Physical combat classes can all use knives, but otherwise stick to their own weapon types, and learn specials that need those types of specials. Spearmen learn to be good at protecting their comrades during combat, Archers rapidly learn elemental arrow attacks and so on.
Edit
:
I am quite sure that you are fully capable of doing random treasure chests, so didn't mention them. If you wanted to compare what you do with what I use, let me know and I will do a few screenshots of the events.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
So... you're looking to play a roguelike that's an RPG?
A lot of what you mention is already feasible within RPG Maker through either "a lot of work" or "grab a plugin".
The things that are "less possible" would be story elements and perhaps "random starts".  Random starts might not be as feasible as if they were truly random, you might start as a Level 1 in a Level 80 area and then you just have to scrap that run.  If you have to "set the spawn", then it won't take very long for you to "have seen all starting positions".
Unfortunately, designing a game like a MadLib is going to be... beyond complicated.  It will stretch into the territory of "impossible to make something coherent".
Just as an example of some of what you're looking for:
"I don't want to know how to complete every quest".
Look up "Elin".
This game has such a system for quests.  "Bring me a [random item] for my [random gender, child]'s birthday!
Cue quests where a parent asks you to bring "a poop" for a gift for their kid.  Or, other random inappropriate stuff.
Imagine that the ending to your game is now "The BBEG can only be defeated with [random item]!" and the random item is... a rock.
Sort of kills the threat of the enemy at the end, does it not?  Any random rock can defeat the BBEG now!
If you want anything resembling coherency and not just a fever dream experienced while high on mushrooms and maybe amphetemines...  You'll have to program in "limits".  Any limit you impose WILL tell you how to complete quests and what the story will be, since it can only be drawn from your carefully crafted list of "sane answers" to any given "problem" the game presents you with.
Put simply, a "truly random" game would be technically possible.  Probably even in RPG Maker with enough time and effort.  Whether the finished product actually is coherent and/or fun... would be quite another matter entirely.
I suspect that should you get exactly what you're asking for, code it, and then play it... you won't want it, and will probably regret having spent the time to make it.
What you're probably looking for is "just a new life to live".  It's the basis for quite a few Isekai anime.  You want all the "random" of the real world, but you can't just start in a new world again, and do whatever it is you like and have the world around you do its own thing without your input.  This is a much harder game to design than a truly random one.
Anyway, yeah... what you want is possible.  Lots of games on the market already do it, usually "in part".  You can see how it works in those games and then figure out how its programmed and mash them together (as well as see what kind of games those end up being with those random features).
I suspect there's a very good reason these systems are only used "in part".  The main reason might be "eats up a lot of ram/memory to have these systems".
Anyway, I'll touch on some of it from a personal standpoint:
I am trying to create a "true choice" game.  The reason for that?  I want to see what stories the PLAYERS will end up with, rather than me (I can write a book, after all, if I want that).  To that end, I have choices that impact a different level of each playthrough.
Main Quest Choices
- Determines the path the character you play as, takes to get to the end.  Branches out, then comes back in to a limited amount of "endings" based on the choices made.
Character Choices
- Determines the state of each party member by the end of the game.  These can subtly shift their personalities or drastically shift their goals and outlooks by the end.
World Choices
- Determines the state of the world by the end of the game, as well as the state of the world you are currently interacting with (these are two different worlds).
Quest Choices
- Determines the state of NPC's and their Quests.  These can have "knock on" effects where their Quests open up more quests, or change what you have access to for gear, or what-have-you.
Personal Choices
- Affects how you interact with combat and minor challenges in the world.  It's as simple as dumping 5 points into Attack or as complicated as equipping a ring that only allows you to do damage via critical hit.
What this means in practice is that at nearly any state of the game, players are all branched off in separate paths.  They might "stay together" for a while, but the deeper you go, the less likely it is that you've made all the exact same choices as any other player has made.
Sure, the initial choice of the game gives you 3 options, but the next choice gives you another 3 based on the first three.  Until I get far enough in, that the choices start "condensing" back down to the finite endings.  But, maybe you tackled a Quest in a specific way, so you have access to a different Quest than other players do.  Or, maybe your character's personalities are a bit different because of the choices you made.  Maybe your characters play differently than those of another player.
Each choice affects the outcome of the gameplay and the ending.  I know what all the endings are and how the player gets there.
But, the surprise is in seeing how the player got there, and what decisions they made to get to that point.
It's a "Choose Your Own Adventure" game.  Except there are no "dead ends" or "return to the start".  Just the story you chose to have to get to the end.
I find more value in seeing what my players will do, rather than trying to see what I will do, when the game gets unhinged and random.
People surprise me.  Systems don't.

posts.author: ZombieKidzRule
posts.body:
@Tai_MT
Thanks for your thoughts! Just to clarify and reiterate a couple of things.
I wouldn't say roguelike exactly if that definition includes the aspect of procedural generation of the game. I think of procedural generation as the entire maps are generated each time (like Dungeon Hack - which was actually a cool game I enjoyed) rather than small aspects being different but the majority of the "maps" are still the same. But if procedural generation doesn't have to be everything, then I think that is probably accurate. I really like D&D inspired, turn-based games.
As I stated earlier, any randomness that would be implemented would have to be within what is considered reasonable which varies from person to person. Since I am making the game that I want to play, I would use my own reasonableness as guide posts, which I know what be everyone's cup of tea so to speak.
I wouldn't suggest doing 100% random starts within a game. Rather, there would be a list of possible starting points to avoid exactly what you are pointing out with starting a game somewhere that would be inappropriate. But from my perspective, having even a handful of starting locations and possible some randomness in what each starting location actually looks like is still better than a 100% fixed game (not that I don't like 100% fixed games - I enjoy those too).
And randomness in quests would also still need reasonableness with lists of what can be combined. Of course that makes it so I, as the developer and player, still know the bookends of what is possible, but I wouldn't know the EXACT solution for any specific play through, which is part of what I'm looking for. Some quests might not have any randomness. It would depend on the quest.
While I would absolutely LOVE a well-crafted, completely procedural generated entire game world, I know that is entirely outside of my capabilities for a hobby game. Instead, I am focusing on things that can add variety and make it so I, and a player, don't experience essentially the same game with a restart. As long as it stays within the scope of what I can do.
I also want the concept of the branching choices matter aspect. I think that most choices (again within reason) in a game should have some sort of impact on your game experience. And that impact can be subtle or significant.
I would also say that since I am approaching this as a hobby and I enjoy learning how to do these sorts of things, I am less focused on the end product and more on the journey. If I have fun experimenting with these sorts of things and end up never actually finishing and releasing such as game, I would still be ok with that. I am at an age where I realize that I have less time in front of me than I have behind me.
@Piyan Glupak
Yes, I didn't specifically list choices in party composition, but that would definitely be part of it. I absolutely LOVE lots of choices in character or party creation. I didn't list it originally because I was thinking that every game would offer the same choices for character/party creation rather than different players experiencing different options. Which is why I only mentioned randomness in recruitible party members. But the character/party creation process can definitely be a part.
And yes about the treasure as well. I would have very few fixed treasure options and those would only be if it was necessary for some sort of quest or the story line. Or if it is certain special equipment that is class specific and you want to make sure that a player has access to those items. I'm thinking of how Wizardry 8 does it for Bards and Gadgeteers. Those classes have special equipment that only they can use and the game has certain items for them in fixed places to ensure availabilty. However, with a little planning and ingenuity, even that could be randomized a bit with checks about where you start, what you already have, etc.
I don't think many of these things are all that hard to incorporate, it just requires forethought, planning, and an interest in implement them. But I can also imagine why some of these things wouldn't necessarily be high priority for commercial games and I'm sure there are many players that wouldn't like many of these concepts in the games they want to play.
@Crim_T
Thanks for those thoughts! I will have to check out the SAGA series.
@ThatIndieSphinx
Thanks for those thoughts as well! I have done some preliminary experiments with randomly connecting maps which I want to pursue further.
Thanks for these responses! This is all part of my planning phase for my future RPG while I'm working on my other project and learning Javascript. I will experiment with many of these in that process as well.

Thanks for your thoughts! Just to clarify and reiterate a couple of things.

"Procedural Generation" can apply to more than just map design.  As an example, a lot of what you're proposing "be random" is actually procedural generation.  Random town names?  Procedural Generation.  Random ingredients to make specific potions?  Procedural Generation.  A lot of Roguelikes actually do this.
ADOM (Ancient Domains of Mystery) actually does some of this.  A "Bubbling Potion" in one game might be a paralysis one.  In the next game, it might be Acid.  This system exists in the game so that "Scrolls of Identify" are always useful, in every single run of the game.  So, basically all items work this way.  Once you "know" what the item is, you generally always know it once you see it.  If you identify the "Crumbling Parchment" as a "Scroll of Identify", then the game tells you every time you run into one, that it's "Scroll of Identify".  But, maybe in your next run, the "Scroll of Identify" is actually an "ink blotted note".
Anyway, a lot of the "random" you're proposing is actually "procedural generation".

This is decently easy to do, even in RPG Maker.  At game start, have it roll a random number for a variable, each variable number teleports the player to the specific map you want (added bonus is that you can have like 6 separate locations with 8 variations, and just have the variable roll 1-48, and then anytime you "walk into" that location, it just remembers you rolled a 27, and teleports you to map 27, because of the conditional branch).

Just going based on what you've described as clarification, it isn't "outside your capabilities", unless you mean, "It's just going to eat up a lot of time to make".  Most of what you describe is just "roll random number for variable, use conditional branches that reference the variable".

This... you might not want to make random or procedural at all.  From a writing standpoint, it's very difficult to get an audience to care when you design something purposefully.  It will be much more difficult if you are allowing "the game" to try to do it for you.
ZombieKidzRule said:

If I have fun experimenting with these sorts of things and end up never actually finishing and releasing such as game, I would still be ok with that. I am at an age where I realize that I have less time in front of me than I have behind me.
Click to expand...
I think aside from things like "item names", which would require plugins, almost everything you've mentioned is handled with variables and conditional branches.  So, I'm not sure how much "learning" you might end up doing with such a project.
Heck, the way you describe wanting your systems to work... I already use a couple systems in this exact same way.
Chest Unlocks
My "thief" can unlock certain chests in the game.  He will annouce the "difficulty" of the chest, but never fail to open it.  The "difficulty" affects the "roll" you make against the chest.  The "roll" can determine what you get out of the chest (each chest has 5 different rewards, based on the Agility stat + roll you make).
Trvial - Adds 1-10 to the "Agility" stat.
Easy - Adds 1-8 to the "Agility" stat.
Medium - Adds 1-6 to the "Agility" stat.
Hard - Adds 1-4 to the "Agility" stat.
Impossible - Adds 0-2 to the "Agility" stat.
An example chest might look like this:
"Thief Roll" = 1-30
>Add Item "Falchion"
"Thief Roll" = 31-40
>Add Item "Hi-Potion"
"Thief Roll" = 41-45
>Add Item "Elixir"
"Thief Roll" = 46-50
>Add Item "Razor Wind"
"Thief Roll" = 51 or more
>Add Item "Infinity +1 Sword"
My "Pillage" skill works the same as the "Thief" rolls, except you get "more consumables" or "different consumables" instead of items.
Likewise, the "best" things to get from each chest aren't always gained from "the highest option", either.  Sometimes, the good stuff is buried close to the bottom or the middle of the list.  So, players who aren't utilizing the Thief for anything except the skill for chests, can and will still get some good loot.  The "roll" can also push you from one reward to another reward, if it's close enough to the edge.
Inn Stays
Random events happen at my Inns.  Or, rather, the characters are placed around the Inn "when you wake up" and you can talk to them to pick up new quests, or learn new things about them.  Each night, the game "rolls" on the table of variables available, and each character in your party is assigned that number, and will be in a different location at the Inn or have different dialogue for you based on that roll.  The hard part was simply getting the game to "don't roll duplicates".  If you've seen the scene before, or got the information, it can't come up again.  I did this through tracking a few variables intead of just 1 and using "math" to suss it out.
Dungeon Layouts
A few of my dungeons will "change layout" based upon different things.  The first dungeon, "Poisonous Mines" changes based upon which party member you recruit first (which one is recruited is based upon the first story choice you made).  So, there's a different layout for having your Wife with you or having your Best Friend with you... as well as which boss you'll fight at the end of that dungeon.
This is just a simple "conditional branch".  In the case of the first dungeon, I have it check "which story choice was picked" to decide which dungeon layout to use (so if a player tries to be clever, and wait until later when they have both party members, the game won't use the incorrect dungeon layout).

posts.body:
RNG applied to story limits the depth of the story... but can make replay interesting.
RNG applied to drops and treasures... can make each game play differently, but adds an element of chaos to team development and power level, which can overstress game balance.
RNG applied to challenges and encounters... can add a feel of true adventure, but can also create a feeling that nothing really matters.
RNG applied to maps can make many maps seem more interesting, but eventually tends to make maps feel lifeless and without purpose.
Essentially... RNG is awesome for replay purposes, but needs to be modified so that games don't go lunatic mode on balance, or on the flipside, become lifeless after a short while.  Players should not
feel
like they are stuck in a procedural loop while they play.
One thing that can be done with a system that includes random chests is to track the quantity opened, and have it increase the reward according to how many are opened.
I've never seen it before.. but it would be possible make "World Encounters" your only random encounters in the game at an extremely low rate... taken from the whole of all troops... but awarding high or escalating per number you defeat.  A player would need to be introduced to it so they don't fight an end game creature (by chance) early on and rage quit.  If they know... they can escape, or maybe avoid?  World encounter troops could only be defeated one time, or only escalate the reward variable on 1st defeat.  In this way.. it becomes like a hunt or challenge system.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
@ZombieKidzRule
There's nothing wrong with "learning by doing".  I was just wondering how much you might learn based on the simple descriptions you were giving for things (obviously if you have a system in place that makes things more complicated, that's something altogether different).  The description of what you wanted were just things that you'd design by doing this:
Conditional Branch
>If [Variable 1] = 15
>>Teleport Player to [X,Y]
>Else
>>Teleport PLayer to [X+1,Y+1]
I do always recommend newbies play heavily with variables and switches.  You can do a lot of insane things with variables.  I prefer the usage of variables over switches for just about everything!  They're a multi-purpose switch!
Anyway, I'm not sure how "impressive" my Inn idea is.  I'd like to streamline it better.  3 variables to make it work is clunky and is "limiting" to some degree.
Here's basically how it works:
Variable 1 tracks "set of numbers that can be rolled"
Variable 2 tracks "total number rolled"
Variable 3 is used to "roll randomly"
So, just as an example, I have 3 options for "random events to be rolled" in the first set.  Variable 1 tracks "hey, first set hasn't been all used up yet, so this doesn't advance".  Variable 3 rolls random number between 1-3.  Let's say it rolls a 2.  Variable two goes up by 2 (0+2).  So, all characters do their "2" set of dialogue/quests/whatever.  Stay the night at the Inn again, let's say you roll a 2 again.  Well, the system checks with Variable 2 to see what it says.  If it says "2", then it rerolls.  Let's say it rolls a 3 after a single reroll.  Variable 2 then adds 3 (2+3=5) to be 5.  Stay the night at the Inn again?  Roll a third time.  It checks against Variable 2.  Since variable 2 = 5...  Anytime a 2 or a 3 are rolled, it will roll again.  Until it rolls 1.  Once that 1 is rolled, Variable 1 will add 1 to its number, so it's now on "Set 2", and the next set of variables can be rolled.
Here's where it gets... messy.
What if a player never stays at an Inn until they've finally got all the party members in the game?  Well, now I need dialogue and stuff for every party member.  Or, what if the player stays at the Inn with 1 party member?
How do I tackle "missing dialogue" or "missing events"?
Conditional Branches.
I make the "Priority Interactions" into Conditionals.  The game checks for every specific story beat and level milestone for each character, before the "dice roll" works on them.  So, you can't miss out on a "Quest Offering" or anything important.  But, "random lore" can be missed out on.
Even more fun?
What do the characters say/do if there's no more dialogue to be had?  I have a page that just rolls "random number" when you talk to them and they'll give you a random piece of dialogue unconnected to the system.
What I actually need to make it work better is just a way to "store used variables" somewhere per character.  Or, in general.  If I had a better way to "eliminate used options", then the player couldn't miss out on anything.  I could probably even offer "more random bits" at a time.
But, the way it is set up now, allows the entire layout of the room to change so that I can set up instances of "characters talking to each other, and you just listening" or whatever.  Maybe this time your Wife is next to the fireplace.  Maybe next time, the resident Thief and his girlfriend are in front of it.
It's not as versatile as I'd like, but it does the job in the very limited way I require that job be done.
EDIT:  Just in case there are questions, I do have a separate variable that "tracks number of rolls made" as well, so that the math works out proper (so if you roll a 1 and a 2, the system isn't erroneously rerolling 3's that you roll, and giving you a 1 or a 2 again).  It's very... messy.
